## How? ##

Use in-built R functions, for example:

```{r sim-data, echo=TRUE}
rand_norm <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 0, sd = 1)
```

::: {.fragment}

```{r plot-sim-data, echo=FALSE}
# use in built R functions, for example:
rand_norm |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=value)) +
  geom_histogram(fill="hotpink", colour="black")
```

:::

## Benefits ##

[Lisa Debruine](debruine.github.io/talks/EMPSEB-fake-it-2023/) outlines these benefits:

1. Develop an understanding of data and statistical concepts.
2. Plan your pre-registration. 
3. Estimate power/precision for a future study.
4. Deal with potential confidentiality issues. 
5. Create demo data for teaching and tutorials.


## Resources ##

- A list of resources that justify the use of fake data from Andrew Gelman [here](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2019/03/23/yes-i-really-really-really-like-fake-data-simulation-and-i-cant-stop-talking-about-it/).

- The [faux](https://debruine.github.io/faux/) R package and some [slides](https://debruine.github.io/talks/EMPSEB-fake-it-2023/#/title-slide) by Lisa Debruine.

- Blog posts by Solomon Kurz [here](https://solomonkurz.netlify.app/blog/bayesian-power-analysis-part-i/).

- R code showing demo examples from my lab [here](https://github.com/rich-ramsey/sim_demo).

- A journal [paper](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2515245920965119) on understanding multi-level regression models via data simulation.
